studies.title: What God Made Lawful
studies.meaning: The Quran opens a surah by questioning its own messenger, which is worth registering before anything else. He had made something unlawful for himself that God had not made unlawful, out of a wish to please his household, and the question asks why. The classical accounts of what was renounced differ, and the surah does not say. Then the correction is softened twice: the ayah ends with two names of mercy, and the next line provides for the releasing of oaths, so the way back is given before any fault is dwelt on.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the later years, and the reports about the occasion vary considerably. Some describe a private renunciation of something permitted; others describe an oath sworn in the same spirit. The classical commentators record more than one account and several name the individuals involved, though the surah itself names no one. What is common to every version is a domestic situation inside the household of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), handled by revelation rather than by anyone present.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb meaning to declare something off limits, from a root that also gives the words for the sacred precinct and the sacred months. What is set apart is put beyond reach, whether by honour or by prohibition.

A noun for someone's satisfaction, used elsewhere in the Quran of seeking God's pleasure. Its appearance here, applied to a household, is what makes the question sharp: a good motive is named and still questioned.
A noun from the verb to untie, the opposite of the word for binding. It names the provision by which an oath can be lifted, and its placement here turns a correction into an exit.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Oaths were load-bearing in Arabian life and were sworn easily. A man swore not to speak to a relative, not to enter a house, not to eat a thing, often in the heat of an evening, and then lived inside the sentence for years because breaking it was worse. Whole feuds were maintained by oaths nobody wanted any more. A recognised procedure for release was a practical mercy in a society that talked itself into corners.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah is named for the verb in its opening line, which appears in the Quran mostly in passages about food, sacred months and family ties. Here it is used of something the Prophet did to himself rather than of anything decreed. The Quran preserves the correction in its own text, which is one of several places where a gentle correction addressed to the messenger is kept rather than removed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things sit together here that rarely do. The messenger is corrected in the text he is delivering, which is a strong argument for the text not being his own composition, and the correction is issued about an act of self-denial undertaken to keep peace at home. What the passage establishes is that restriction is not automatically piety. Something permitted stays permitted, and closing it off for a good reason is still closing off what was given.

crossReferences.why: Tells believers not to forbid the good things God has made lawful for them.
Sets out the expiation by which an oath can be released, which this passage refers to.
Asks who has forbidden the adornment and good provision God brought out for His servants.

studies.applyIt: Look at one rule you have made for yourself that nobody asked for: the food you avoid, the thing you will not accept, the pleasure you have decided is not for you. Ask where it came from. If the honest answer is that it keeps someone else comfortable, consider letting it go this week. The ayah does not praise the self-denial. It asks why.

studies.title: Part Told, Part Left
studies.meaning: A confidence was given and did not stay. What the ayah records next is a piece of conduct worth slowing down for: when the disclosure became known to him, he mentioned part of what he had learned and turned away from part. He did not present the whole of what he knew. The commentators read the omission as deliberate restraint, a refusal to use everything available in a confrontation. The exchange then closes with a question and an answer that changes the subject entirely: who told you.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The classical sources give differing accounts of what was said and to whom, and several name the people involved; the surah itself says only that it was one of his wives. That reticence is the text's own choice, and the commentators who name names do so from later reports rather than from the passage. What the ayah preserves is the shape of the episode, not its cast.

keyTerms.note: A verb for entrusting something to one person alone, from the root that gives the word for a secret. It names an act of trust rather than concealment, which is what makes the sequel matter.
A verb for turning the side of oneself toward something, used of deliberately not engaging. Here it describes information withheld rather than a person avoided, which is an unusual and specific use.
The ordinary word for a piece of speech or a new thing said, from a root meaning newness. The Quran leaves the content unspecified, so the word names an event of speaking rather than any subject.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Information moved fast in Medina and was the main currency of influence. Households were adjacent, women visited between them daily, and what one person knew at noon several knew by dusk. There were no closed rooms in the modern sense. Keeping a confidence in that setting was a genuine discipline rather than a formality, and everyone listening to this ayah had either broken one or watched one broken.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah uses four different forms of the same root for informing, in four positions: she informed, he informed her, who informed you, the All-Knowing informed me. Arabic allows this kind of repetition to carry an argument, and here it moves the act of telling up a chain until the last one has no human source at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage models a use of knowledge rather than stating a rule about it. Someone who had been wronged in a small, private way, and who had complete information about it, chose to say less than he could. That restraint is recorded in scripture, which gives it the status of instruction without ever phrasing it as one. The closing line adds the other half: the source of what he knew was not investigation, and he says so plainly.

crossReferences.why: Asks those with means to pardon and overlook, and whether they would not like God's forgiveness.
Warns against spying and against speaking of one another behind their backs.
States that God does not like the public voicing of grievance, except from one who is wronged.

studies.applyIt: The next time you are in the right and know something that would settle it, say half of what you have. Keep the rest. Not as leverage, and not to seem gracious: simply do not use it. The ayah records a man who had every fact and told part. Notice how much of the wish to be fully vindicated survives the experiment.

studies.title: If The Two Of You Turn
studies.meaning: The ayah is addressed to two people in the dual, a grammatical form English cannot reproduce, and it offers them a way back before it describes anything else. The clause about hearts is read in two ways by the commentators, either as a statement that the hearts have already inclined away, which is why repentance is called for, or as a promise about what turning will do. Then the alternative is named and answered with a list of supporters so large that the point is not the outcome but the disproportion.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The surah is addressing a disagreement inside a household, and the reports about who was involved differ; the text uses the dual without naming anyone. The commentators discuss the identity of the righteous believers named among the supporters and give several readings without agreement. What the passage plainly does is offer the turning first and describe the alternative second.

keyTerms.note: A verb for tilting, used of a vessel that leans and of an ear turned to listen. The image is a slight deviation from upright rather than a fall, which keeps the fault small and correctable.

A reciprocal verb from the root for the back, meaning to support one another as two people leaning back to back. It names an alliance rather than an act, which is what the ayah then answers with a longer list.

A word for the party who stands behind someone in a dispute, covering patron, ally and guardian. In that society a man without one had no recourse, so naming God in the role settles the question of standing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Backing was literal in Arabian disputes. Two men standing back to back could not be surrounded, and the word for that posture became the word for alliance. When a quarrel escalated, everyone present counted who stood where, and the count decided the outcome before anything was said. This ayah is written into that arithmetic. It responds to a pair by naming a list, in the form a seventh-century listener would have heard as a tally.
studies.didYouKnow: Gabriel is named explicitly in only three places in the Quran, and this is one of them; elsewhere he appears by description rather than by name. The ayah also uses the dual form throughout its first half, a number Arabic marks separately from singular and plural, which lets the address stay precise without naming anyone.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The order of the two halves is the argument. Repentance is offered before the alternative is described, so the door is open before the consequence is named, and that is the Quran's habitual sequence in passages of correction. The list of supporters then does something subtler than threaten. It tells a person in a private quarrel that they are not the only party present, which is a claim about the scale of an ordinary disagreement.

crossReferences.why: Names Gabriel as the one who brought the revelation down upon the heart, one of the few namings.
Describes God and the angels sending blessings upon the Prophet, a similar gathering of support.
Calls people to turn back to their Lord and submit before the punishment arrives upon them.

studies.applyIt: Notice when you start recruiting. The moment a disagreement with one person becomes a search for someone who agrees with you, something has changed, and it usually changes before you notice. This week, when you catch yourself about to tell a third person your side, stop and go back to the first one instead. The ayah offers the turn before anything else.

studies.title: A List Of Qualities
studies.meaning: The ayah is conditional twice over and never becomes a statement of fact. It begins with a particle of possibility and continues with an if, so nothing is announced and nothing happens. What the line actually contains is a list: six qualities, each a participle, describing what better would consist of. The commentators note that the list is entirely inward apart from the last pair, so the standard being set is devotional rather than social. The word rendered as fasting is read by several as also meaning travelling for God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The ayah belongs to a passage addressed to a household in a difficult week, and the reports around it vary. The commentators are careful with it. They note that the possibility named never came about, that the conditional particle keeps it hypothetical, and that the list which follows became, in later devotional writing, a description of qualities to aim for rather than a comparison between people.

keyTerms.note: A particle of hope and possibility, not of prediction. Placed at the head of the sentence it governs everything after it, so the whole ayah describes something that might happen rather than something announced.
A participle for standing in sustained attentiveness before God, associated in the Quran with long prayer and quiet constancy. It describes a posture held over time rather than an act performed once.

A participle from a root meaning to travel or to flow. Classical commentators read it here mostly as fasting, on the reasoning that a faster moves through the day without provision, and they preserve the travelling sense alongside it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Marriage in Arabia was arranged between families and assessed by the things families could count: lineage, property, the alliances a match would create, the standing of a woman's brothers. Nobody's list of qualities began with devotion. The six words in this ayah name almost nothing a negotiating family would have raised, which is what made the line strange to its first hearers before it became familiar to later ones.
studies.didYouKnow: The qualities in this ayah arrive as a chain of feminine plural forms, seven of them ending in the same syllable, before the final word breaks the rhyme. Arabic rhetoric uses this kind of accumulation for emphasis, and the Quran employs it sparingly. Here it produces a list that can be memorised in a single hearing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What the list does is relocate worth. Every quality named is available to anyone and none of them is inherited, so the standard set is one a person can move toward rather than one they are born into or excluded from. And the conditional framing matters theologically as much as grammatically: the ayah does not declare anyone replaced. It describes what better would mean, which leaves the description standing long after the moment that produced it.

crossReferences.why: Gives a longer list of the same kind, applied to men and women together in matching pairs.
States that the most honoured with God is the most mindful, removing lineage as the measure.
Lists qualities of the believers in the same participial form, including the word read as fasting here.

studies.applyIt: Pick one quality from this list and give it fifteen minutes tomorrow: the turning back, the standing attentively, the doing without. Not as a programme. Once, to see what it is like from inside. The ayah lists qualities rather than achievements, and qualities are things you can practise for a quarter of an hour and learn something true about.

studies.title: Yourself First, Then Your House
studies.meaning: The instruction begins with the self and extends outward to the household, in that order. Nothing is said about how, which the commentators fill in with teaching and example rather than with force. Then the fire is described by two details: its fuel, which includes stones, and its keepers, angels described as harsh and strong and defined entirely by not deviating from what they are told. The next line cuts off appeal on the day itself.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The surah is short, and its opening ayat deal with a private matter inside the household of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) that became public. The address then widens from that house to every believing house. No set occasion is reported for these two ayat. Early writers read the widening as the shape of the surah. A family matter is followed by an order to every family.

keyTerms.note: A two-letter imperative from the root behind God-consciousness, which also means to place a barrier between something and harm. The word is a shield before it is a warning.
The word for what is burned rather than for the burning. Naming stones alongside people is unusual, and early scholars connect it to what was carved and worshipped rather than to ordinary rock.
Two adjectives of physical toughness, used of rough cloth and of hard ground. Neither describes cruelty. They describe an absence of softness, which the clause about never deviating then explains.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A household in Medina was bigger than a modern family. Parents, children, relatives without means and often servants all lived inside one compound. Duty ran with authority. The head of the house answered in public for what happened under his roof. This order uses that structure and changes what it holds. What a man answered for became what his household believed, not only what it did.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about a fire whose fuel is people and stones appears twice in the Quran. It is here, and near the start of the longest surah, in the same words. The lines about the angels are the Quran's plainest statement of what angels are. They are beings with no gap at all between the order and the act.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Duty reaches past the self here without turning into force. The verb is one of shielding, and the object is a family. So a person is held answerable for people whose choices are not his to make. The tradition settles this by placing the duty in teaching and example, not in the result. The angels then stand as a contrast. They are the only beings in the passage with no gap between what they are told and what they do.

crossReferences.why: Carries the same description of the fire, in identical words, near the opening of the longest surah.
Gives the practical shape of the same responsibility, instruction to the household paired with the speaker's own practice.
Describes angels in the same terms, acting only on command and never in front of it.

studies.applyIt: Do one thing this week that your household will notice you doing rather than hear you asking for. Read something out loud where they can hear it, or keep a small commitment you had been letting slide. The ayah puts yourself first in the sentence and the family second, and the order is not accidental.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people to guard themselves and their families from a fire. Angels stand over that fire and do exactly what God tells them. On that day, no one will be allowed to make excuses.

studies.title: Repentance That Sews It Shut
studies.meaning: One word qualifies the repentance, and early scholars wrote at length about it. Their readings range from sincere, to thorough, to the kind that mends. What follows is not a promise but a strong hope, carried by a particle of expectation. Then the scene shifts. Light runs ahead of people and to their right. Their prayer is not for entry. They ask for the light to be completed, which suggests it arrives partial.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a surah that has just described a private disagreement made public and a warning to households. No set occasion is reported for this ayah. It is the turn in the surah. After two ayat about the fire and its keepers, the address comes back to the believers with an order that assumes they have something to repent for. That is the surah's premise about everyone in it.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from a root meaning to advise honestly and to sew a tear closed. Both senses are recorded: repentance that is candid with itself, and repentance that repairs what was torn.
A verb meaning to cover something so it is no longer seen, from the same root as covering seed with soil. What is promised is that the deed is hidden, not a claim that it never happened.
An imperative asking for something already begun to be finished. The prayer treats the light as real and as not enough at once, which is why early scholars hear worry in it rather than confidence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Night travel in Arabia was done by starlight. A party crossing open ground kept together by whatever light it had. A lamp carried at the front lit a few paces and no more. You walked inside a small moving ring of light with darkness on every side. Asking for a light to be completed was asking for what a traveller had wanted on every night journey.
studies.didYouKnow: The word that qualifies repentance here occurs only once in the whole Quran. That is part of why so much was written about it. Early scholars gathered dozens of definitions and kept several of them. The word had no other use in the Quran to fix its meaning against.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah asks for a whole-hearted act and guarantees no outcome. That is a particular arrangement. Hope comes with a particle, so nothing is owed. The order itself carries no conditions. The closing scene holds the same balance. People already walking in light still pray for more of it. Nobody in the passage is finished, and that is shown as the normal state of a believer, not as a failure.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same scene from the other side, with people outside the light asking to borrow it.
Removes the ceiling this ayah's particle of hope might seem to imply, promising forgiveness without qualification.
Puts the same instruction in the plural at the end of a passage about conduct, addressed to everyone at once.

studies.applyIt: Repentance in this ayah is described as something that mends. So pick the one thing your turning away actually damaged, and repair a piece of it this week: the apology, the money, the conversation you have been avoiding. Feeling sorry is not the part the word describes. Sewing the tear is.
studies.explainEasier: God tells people to turn back to him and mean it. He says their wrongs may then be covered over, and they may enter gardens. On that day, light runs in front of them, and they ask God to make it full.

studies.title: Firmness Without Softening
studies.meaning: A short instruction addressed to the messenger alone, and the commentators are careful about its scope. The verb for striving is the general one and does not specify a means; classical readers took it here as sustained effort in argument and proclamation toward the first group, and as firmness rather than force toward the second, since the hypocrites of Medina were never fought. The word for sternness names the removal of accommodation, not cruelty. The ayah then closes with their end, which is left to God rather than to anyone present.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The same sentence appears earlier in the Quran, in a surah from the late Medinan period, with identical wording. The commentators note the repetition and read the second occurrence as placed for its position rather than for a new occasion, closing a passage about a household by widening to the community. No specific incident is attached to it.

keyTerms.note: An imperative from the root meaning effort to capacity, with no object of means attached. Arabic leaves the method open, which is why classical readers specify it differently according to who is being addressed.

A verb from the root for thickness or coarseness, the opposite of the word for gentleness. It describes the withdrawal of softness in manner rather than the infliction of harm, and the same root names a rough garment.
A noun for the place a person takes refuge in, used of a nest and of a home returned to at night. Applying it to the fire is a hard irony, since the word ordinarily promises rest.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina in those years ran on accommodation. Alliances crossed families and faiths, agreements were renegotiated constantly, and a leader's usual instrument was conciliation because the alternative fractured the town. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is described in the sources as habitually gentle in manner, which is the background against which an instruction to withdraw softness would have registered as an instruction at all.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah is one of a small set of sentences the Quran repeats word for word in two different surahs. The other occurrence sits in a long passage about a specific expedition; this one closes a chapter about a household. The identical wording in two very different settings is what led classical commentators to read the striving as taking different forms in each.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah is addressed to one person holding public responsibility, which the classical reading keeps in view. It does not authorise a reader to identify anyone as belonging to either group, and the Quran elsewhere reserves that knowledge to God. What it establishes is that gentleness is a means rather than an end: there are situations in which continued accommodation becomes its own kind of failure, and firmness is the honest response. The verdict itself is never handed over.

crossReferences.why: Contains the same sentence word for word, inside a passage about a specific campaign.
Says it was by a mercy from God that he was gentle, and that harshness would have scattered them.
States that some among the desert Arabs and the people of Medina are not known to the Prophet.

studies.applyIt: Think of a situation where you keep being pleasant because the alternative is uncomfortable, and the pleasantness has stopped helping anyone. Say the plain thing once this week, without heat and without apology afterwards. The ayah asks for the removal of softness, not for anger. Those are different, and most people who try this discover they had confused them.

studies.title: Married To A Prophet
studies.meaning: Two examples are given and the point of both is negative: proximity did not transfer. The women named were inside the households of two prophets, described here simply as righteous servants, and the word used for what they did is betrayal, which the commentators are unanimous in reading as a betrayal of trust and message rather than of the marriage bed. What is stated plainly is the outcome: the two men availed them nothing. The Quran raises the strongest possible case of connection in order to remove it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and the placement is pointed: the surah has been addressing a household, and it closes with examples drawn from other households. The commentators note that the two women are named only by their relation, which keeps the example about the position rather than the person. They also note the pairing that follows, two examples of belief in equally difficult settings, so the surah gives both directions.

keyTerms.note: A verb for breaking a trust, the opposite of keeping something entrusted. Classical commentators state explicitly that no prophet's wife was ever unfaithful, and read the word here of concealment and of siding against the message.
A preposition for position, used idiomatically in Arabic of a woman's place within a marriage. It names proximity and shelter, which is precisely the relation the ayah then says conferred nothing.
From the root meaning to be free of need. To avail someone is to make them not need anything further, and the negation says the connection could not supply what was missing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing in Arabia was largely inherited and married into. A person's protection, credit and reputation came from the household they belonged to, and a good marriage could lift a family for generations. That is what makes these two examples land. They take the most advantageous connection imaginable, a place inside a prophet's household, and report that on the one occasion it mattered most it was worth nothing at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah ends with four women held up as examples, two negative and two positive, and none of them is given a name except the last. The other three are identified by their relation to a man. The Quran's usual practice is to name almost no women at all, so a chapter that closes on four female examples is unusual in its own terms.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage closes a loophole that most religious communities rely on quietly. Being near the centre, married into it, descended from it, sitting in the right room, is described as conferring nothing that can be carried to the end. The examples are chosen for maximum proximity, so no lesser connection can be argued from. What remains after the connection is removed is the person's own position, which is the only thing the ayah treats as theirs.

crossReferences.why: Tells Noah that his son is not of his family, because his conduct was not righteous.
States that no bearer of burdens carries the burden of another, however close the two are.
Says that on that day nothing avails except coming to God with a sound heart.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you would be tempted to mention if you had to account for yourself: who you are related to, what institution you belong to, whose student you were. Now set it aside and write one sentence about what you actually do with your week. The ayah removes every borrowed credential and leaves exactly that sentence standing.

studies.title: A House Near You
studies.meaning: The example set for believers is a woman inside the household of the man the Quran uses as its type of tyranny. Her prayer runs in an odd order. The house comes first, and she asks for it near God rather than in the garden. Early scholars read that as asking for nearness before comfort. Then come two rescues: from Pharaoh and his work, and from the wrongdoing people. She names the household and the society apart from each other.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing a surah that began with a domestic matter and ends with four women held up as examples. Two of them are offered as warnings, the wives of Noah and Lot, and two as models, this woman and Mary. No specific occasion is reported for this ayah. The pairing is the surah's argument: proximity to a righteous man saves nobody, and proximity to a tyrant condemns nobody.

keyTerms.note: A builder's imperative, the ordinary verb for putting up a house. She asks for construction rather than admission, which is a request for something made specifically, not for a place among many.
A preposition of nearness and of belonging. Putting it before the mention of the garden makes the place secondary. What she asks for is nearness, and the garden is where that nearness happens to be.

A verb of pulling someone clear of danger, said twice in one short prayer. The repeat splits the man from the people, so she asks to be saved from a marriage and from a society in two separate requests.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The audience for this ayah included women whose households had turned on them when they believed. It included men whose families had done the same. Arab society made a woman's place wholly dependent on her husband and his clan. A wife at odds with her husband's whole world had no way out at all. Pharaoh's wife is the extreme form of what some listeners were living.
studies.didYouKnow: The example is set for those who believe, with no limit attached. So a woman is held up as the model for a whole community, not just for its women. The Quran does the same in the next ayah, with Mary. Both examples close a surah that opened with a disagreement between a man and his wives. Where they sit is the surah's answer to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage cuts the link between where a person lives and where they stand with God. A woman inside the household of the Quran's worst tyrant is named as the model for believers. Nothing is said about her leaving. Her prayer also reorders what people usually ask for. Nearness comes first, the place second, and rescue last. That order describes a faith that is not mainly an escape plan.

crossReferences.why: Sets the opposite case immediately before, two women close to prophets whose closeness availed them nothing.
Completes the pair of examples, adding a woman named for her devotion rather than for her household.
Shows the same woman earlier, intervening inside the same household to save a child from it.

studies.applyIt: Notice the order in this prayer the next time you ask for something. She asks for nearness first and for rescue last, which is the reverse of how most requests come out. Try saying one thing you want in that order, once, tonight: what you want to be near, then what you want out of.
studies.explainEasier: Pharaoh's wife lived in the house of a cruel king. She still asked God for a home near him, and to save her from her husband and from the bad people around her. God holds her up as an example.

studies.title: She Confirmed The Words
studies.meaning: The surah's final example is given four descriptions and none of them is her motherhood. She guarded herself, the spirit was breathed in, she confirmed the words of her Lord and His books, and she was among the devout. The commentators note the grammar of that last phrase: the plural used is masculine, so she is placed among a group rather than in a category of her own. What the ayah praises is belief and constancy, with the extraordinary event mentioned in the middle and not dwelt on.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Medina had Christian visitors and a community aware of the gospel accounts, and the Quran's portrait of Mary was known and discussed there. The commentators note the placement: after two women who were close to prophets and lost everything, the surah names two who had no such advantage and are held up as examples. The second is presented last and without qualification.

keyTerms.note: A verb from the root for a fortress, meaning to make something secure and inaccessible. The Quran uses the same root for a fortified town, so the word describes protection rather than mere abstention.

From the root for truthfulness, the verb means to declare something true rather than simply to accept it. It makes her belief an act she performed, which is why it is listed alongside what was done to her.

A masculine plural, though it describes a woman, which classical grammarians read as placing her within the whole company of the devout rather than in a separate group. Arabic uses the masculine plural for mixed company.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A woman without a husband and with a child had almost no standing in seventh-century Arabia, and the accusations that followed such a situation were public and permanent. Poets made careers from them. The Quran's audience understood exactly what Mary's position would have cost socially, which is why the surah's decision to end on her, unqualified and last, would have registered as a deliberate reversal of the ordinary ranking.
studies.didYouKnow: Mary is the only woman named in the Quran; every other woman, including the others in this surah's closing examples, is identified by a relationship. Her name appears in the Book more often than the New Testament names her, and a surah is called after her. Here she closes a chapter that began with a correction inside a household.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah describes a person who received something no one else received and then praises her for what she did rather than for what happened to her. Three of the four descriptions are actions: guarding, confirming, belonging to the devout. That ordering has a consequence. It means the example is followable, since nothing being praised is unrepeatable, and the surah has just spent two ayat establishing that connection to greatness transfers nothing.

crossReferences.why: Records that Mary was chosen and purified and chosen above the women of the worlds.
Opens the annunciation account, with her withdrawal to a place apart from her people.
Repeats the same phrase about guarding and the breathing of the spirit, in shorter form.

studies.applyIt: Take something that happened to you that you did not choose, good or hard, and write down what you actually did with it. Not what it meant. What you did. The ayah praises Mary for three actions and mentions the miracle in a single clause between them, which is a way of saying that the part belonging to you is the part worth recording.
